section: six ways to split one training step
text: Six ways to split one training step A training step is a forward pass over a batch, a backward pass that produces one gradient per parameter, and an optimizer update.
label: fat
note: defines a training step, which the reader knows; the hero and section 1 carry what matters

section: six ways to split one training step
text: When the model, its optimizer state or its activations do not fit on one GPU, or one GPU is too slow, the step is cut along one of five dimensions: the batch (data parallelism), the stored state (sharded data parallelism: ZeRO, FSDP), each weight matrix (tensor parallelism), the layers (pipeline parallelism), the experts of a mixture-of-experts model (expert parallelism) or the sequence (context parallelism).
label: core
key: the batch, the stored state, each weight matrix, the layers, the experts or the sequence

section: six ways to split one training step
text: Every cut buys memory or speed with communication, and the communication has a shape (a collective ) and a wire it has to cross: NVLink inside a server, InfiniBand or Ethernet between servers, about nine times slower per GPU on an H100 cluster.
label: core
key: about nine times faster per GPU

section: collectives, and the wire they cross
text: Collectives, and the wire they cross Every split communicates through a handful of operations that all GPUs in a group call together (NCCL implements them on NVIDIA hardware): all-reduce , after which every GPU holds the element-wise sum (gradient averaging in data parallelism, the partial sums in tensor parallelism); reduce-scatter and all-gather , one slice of the sum or every slice (ZeRO and FSDP; a ring all-reduce is exactly a reduce-scatter followed by an all-gather, which is why ZeRO-1 and ZeRO-2 cost what DDP costs, Ultra-Scale Playbook ); all-to-all , a different piece to every GPU (expert dispatch and combine, DeepSpeed Ulysses); and send and receive between pipeline stages.
label: core
key: Expert dispatch and combine; DeepSpeed Ulysses

section: collectives, and the wire they cross
text: In a ring each GPU sends 2( n − 1)/ n of the buffer for an all-reduce and ( n − 1)/ n for the others ( nccl-tests ), so the bytes per GPU barely change with the group size and the slowest link sets the time.
label: core
key: the slowest link sets the time

text: Data parallelism (DP, DDP) Replicate the model on every GPU and give each replica a different micro-batch.
label: core
key: give each replica a different micro-batch

text: After backward, an all-reduce averages the gradients, so every replica takes the identical optimizer step: copy the model to each of the X GPUs; shard the batch; forward in parallel; backward in parallel; all-reduce the gradients, overlapped with backward by sending them in buckets (25 MiB by default in PyTorch, DistributedDataParallel ); the same optimizer step everywhere.
label: core

text: PyTorch's old DataParallel was a single process driving the GPUs of one machine by threads; DDP ( DistributedDataParallel ) runs one process per GPU, works across machines, and is the baseline everything else builds on ( Li et al.
label: core
key: runs one process per GPU, works across machines

text: It is simple and scales nearly linearly while the all-reduce hides behind backward.
label: core
key: scales nearly linearly while the all-reduce hides behind backward

text: Its cost is memory: the full model, gradients and optimizer state on every GPU, 16 bytes per parameter, so a model above about 5B parameters no longer fits on an 80 GB GPU with Adam (80 / 16, derived ).
label: core

text: That ceiling is what ZeRO and FSDP remove.
label: core
key: the ceiling ZeRO and FSDP remove

text: The global batch is micro-batch × gradient-accumulation steps × data-parallel degree ( Playbook ), so DP is also how a layout reaches its target batch once the model fits.
label: core

text: Tensor parallelism and sequence parallelism Tensor parallelism splits individual weight matrices "horizontally" across GPUs ( Megatron-LM ): a column-parallel matrix followed by a row-parallel one, in the feed-forward block and in attention (heads are divided among GPUs), so the nonlinearity in between needs no communication and each block ends with one all-reduce.
label: core

text: That is two all-reduces per layer forward and two backward, inside every layer, in small latency-bound messages.
label: core
key: two all-reduces per layer forward and two backward

text: In the animation TP sends 51.5 GB per GPU for the step, more than any other mode.
label: core
key: 51.5 GB per GPU for this step

text: It therefore needs NVLink-class bandwidth and stays inside a server: Megatron's guidance is TP "up to degree g when using g-GPU servers", then pipeline parallelism across servers ( Narayanan et al.
label: core
key: up to degree g when using g-GPU servers

text: 2021 ), and the Playbook measured "around 43% performance degradation" when TP crosses nodes, against 14% for PP.
label: core

text: Sequence parallelism (Megatron-style) extends TP to the regions TP leaves replicated, LayerNorm and dropout, by splitting their activations along the sequence.
label: core
key: the regions TP leaves replicated, LayerNorm and dropout

text: The all-reduce becomes a reduce-scatter plus an all-gather of the same total size, so communication is unchanged and the duplicated activation memory disappears: activations per layer fall from sbh (34 + 5 as / h ) to sbh / t (34 + 5 as / h ), and with selective recomputation to 34 sbh / t ( Korthikanti et al.

text: Do not confuse it with context parallelism below, which splits the sequence through attention too.
label: core

text: Context parallelism Context parallelism shards the sequence dimension of the activations across GPUs, for long-context training where activation memory, which grows with sequence length, is what no longer fits.
label: core

text: Token-wise layers (the feed-forward block, norms) need nothing from other GPUs; attention does, because every query needs the keys and values of earlier tokens.
label: core
key: every query needs the keys and values of earlier tokens

text: Three ways to supply them: Ring Attention ( Liu et al.
label: core

text: 2023 ): key and value blocks are passed round a ring, each step's transfer overlapped with attention on the block already received.
label: core
key: each overlapped with attention on the block already received

text: DeepSpeed Ulysses ( Jacobs et al.
label: core

text: 2023 ): an all-to-all regroups the data so each GPU holds the full sequence for a subset of heads, computes ordinary attention, and a second all-to-all switches back.
label: core

text: Its communication volume stays constant when sequence length and GPU count grow together, and it trained "2.5x faster with 4x longer sequence length" than the baseline it compared with reported ; because it splits by heads, its degree is bounded by the head count derived .
label: core

text: All-gather , Llama 3's choice: gather all keys and values, then compute attention for the local queries.
label: core

text: The gather is exposed rather than overlapped, but with grouped-query attention keys and values are much smaller than queries and the gather is O( S ) against attention's O( S ²); it also handles document masks easily (§3.3.2).
label: core

text: Causal attention makes late tokens more expensive than early ones, so the sequence is cut into 2 × CP chunks and rank i takes chunks i and 2 × CP − 1 − i (Llama 3; the CP mode above draws it).

label: core

text: Full recomputation (keep only each layer's input) costs 30 to 40% more execution time (36% measured); selective recomputation of only the attention core, the large but cheap part, cuts activation memory about 5 times for 2.7% (GPT-3) or 1.6% (MT-NLG) extra FLOPs ( Korthikanti et al.
label: core

text: Common mistakes "1F1B shrinks the pipeline bubble" It does not: GPipe and 1F1B share the ( p − 1)/ m bubble.
label: core
key: zero-bubble schedules and DualPipe are what shrink the bubble

text: 1F1B caps the activations in flight at p micro-batches.
label: core
key: caps the activations in flight at p micro-batches

text: Interleaving (÷ v ), zero-bubble schedules and DualPipe are what shrink the bubble. "ZeRO-3 is free memory" It costs 1.5 times DP's communication, and with gradient accumulation it gathers the weights for every micro-batch, forward and backward.
label: core
key: gathers the weights again for every micro-batch

text: Across servers that traffic lands on the slow link; HSDP or ZeRO-2 are the usual fixes. "Context parallelism (or expert parallelism) shrinks the weights" Neither does by itself.
label: core
key: HSDP or ZeRO-2 are the usual fixes

text: CP cuts activations; EP spreads experts but each GPU still holds a dense model's worth of state (both modes above stay at 128.5 GB).
label: depth
key: both steps above stay at 128.5 GB

text: They are combined with FSDP, ZeRO-1 or TP for the weights. "Sequence parallelism and context parallelism are the same thing" Megatron's sequence parallelism splits only the regions tensor parallelism leaves replicated (norms, dropout) and lives inside the TP group.
label: depth

text: Context parallelism splits attention itself across its own group and can be used without TP. "Tensor parallelism across servers is just slower" It is much slower: four latency-bound collectives per layer per micro-batch.
label: depth
key: four latency-bound collectives per layer per micro-batch

text: The Playbook measured about 43% degradation crossing nodes, against 14% for pipeline parallelism over the same boundary. "Data parallelism can always use more GPUs" Only while there are sequences to hand out: global batch = micro-batch × accumulation × DP.
label: core
key: a fixed token budget per step caps it

text: A fixed token budget per step caps DP, which is why Llama 3's 16K-GPU run had fewer sequences per DP rank and a lower MFU (41% against 43%, §3.3.2). "16 bytes per parameter is a law" It is the ZeRO paper's convention for bf16 with fp32 Adam.
label: core

text: FP32 gradients make it 18 to 20, bf16 moments 14, an 8-bit optimizer less; activations come on top.
